facts.statement: The genus Platydyptes was described by Marples in 1952.
Fossils of Platydyptes date from the Late Oligocene to the Early Miocene.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Late Oligocene to Early Miocene,

facts.statement: Platydyptes is an extinct genus of penguin that lived in New Zealand between 27.3 and 21.7 million years ago.
facts.quote: Platydyptes is a genus of extinct penguins from the Late Oligocene to Early Miocene (about 27.3 to 21.7 million years ago) of New Zealand.

facts.statement: All three species of Platydyptes were described from fossils found in the north Otago to south Canterbury region of New Zealand's South Island.
facts.quote: It was created by Brian Marples in 1952 and contains three relatively large species, all of which were described from the north Otago to south Canterbury region in the South Island.

facts.statement: The genus name Platydyptes refers to the broad and flat shape of the humerus bone.
facts.quote: The genus name Platydyptes combines the Greek platys ("broad and flat"), alluding to the shape of the humerus, with dyptes ("diver").

facts.statement: Platydyptes amiesi was the largest species, roughly the size of a king penguin but with longer flippers.
facts.quote: Platydyptes amiesi Marples, 1952 – Amies' penguin. The largest species, it was about the size of a king penguin, though with longer flippers.

facts.statement: Platydyptes belongs to the class Aves and the parent group Sphenisciformes.
The time range for Platydyptes is from the Priabonian to the Aquitanian stages, spanning 36.7 to 21.7 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Priabonian to Aquitanian (36.7 to 21.7 million years ago)

rejected.statement: The name Platydyptes amiesi honors A.C. Amies, a University of Otago student who collected the first specimen in 1946.
rejected.quote: The epithet and common name honour A.C. Amies, a University of Otago student who collected the first specimen in 1946 and was killed in Malaysia soon afterwards.
rejected.reason: statement copies the source wording: 'University of Otago student who collected the first'
